113.title: The partly column
113.hook: modern writers, not Epictetus, add a third column: things partly up to me
113.howItsDone: Some modern readers of Stoicism use a three-column sort, following William Irvine: what's fully up to me, what isn't, and what's partly up to me, which they break down until they find the piece that is fully theirs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the archer, who does everything to aim well and lets the wind have the rest. Your line was aim, then let go. What did you aim at, and did you let it go? Day one hundred thirteen.

Try Epictetus's two columns on a real worry, and something awkward happens. Say you're worried about your health. Is that up to you? Not entirely. Genes, accidents, luck. Not up to you at all? That doesn't feel right either: you choose what you eat, whether you walk, whether you see a doctor. Or your kid's grades. Your marriage. Your job. Plenty of the things people actually lie awake about don't fit neatly in either column. They sit somewhere in between. Modern writers noticed this, and some of them drew a third column. Today: the partly column.
screen: `YOUR HEALTH: MINE?` → `NOT ENTIRELY. NOT NOT.` → `A THIRD COLUMN.`

segments.voice: First, the honest history. Epictetus had two columns, not three. The third was added in our own time, notably by the American philosophy professor William Irvine in a 2009 book on Stoic practice, where he called it the trichotomy of control: things we have complete control over, things we have no control over, and things we have some control over. Some Stoic scholars push back. They say Epictetus didn't need a third column, because anything partly up to you can be split into the part that's yours and the part that isn't. And here's the useful thing: if you follow either path carefully, you end up in the same place. Take the tennis match, Irvine's own example. Winning is partly up to you. You can't control your opponent, the wind or the line judge. So what do you do with the partly column? You break it open, and look for the piece that is fully yours: to practice hard, to play as well as you can today. That becomes your goal. Not win, but play my best. Which is exactly Cato's archer from yesterday, aiming well and letting the result go. The partly column isn't a place to leave things. It's a place to open things up. Your health: the walk, the vegetables, the appointment are yours; the rest is not. Your kid's grades: the quiet desk, the encouragement, the patience are yours; the grades are theirs. Find your part. Do your part. Let the rest be the rest.
screen: `EPICTETUS HAD TWO COLUMNS.` · `IRVINE, 2009: A THIRD.` · `BREAK IT OPEN.` · `FIND THE PIECE THAT'S FULLY YOURS.` · then, large: `MY PART ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one partly-mine thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you care about that's partly up to you. Your health, a relationship, a project. Hold it in mind. Now break it open. Ask: what, in this, is fully mine? Maybe one call, one habit, one kind word, one hour. Name it clearly. Then set the rest down beside it, gently: not mine. Breathe with your part in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Trichotomy. William Irvine's name for the third column, what's partly up to you, broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Today's word.
Your line: my part only. Today, when something big and tangled weighs on you, ask: what's my part? Do that part well, and let the rest be the rest. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: Serenity, courage, wisdom
114.hook: a twentieth-century prayer by Reinhold Niebuhr asks for serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart
114.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Serenity Prayer, and Alcoholics Anonymous and other recovery groups often say it aloud together at the close of a meeting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: trichotomy, broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Your line was my part only. What was your part, and did you do it? Day one hundred fourteen.

You may have seen it on a kitchen magnet, or a plaque in a hospital waiting room, or hanging on the wall of a church basement where folding chairs are set out in a circle. A short prayer, three lines long, said aloud in rooms like that one. In one breath, it says much of what we've been learning from Epictetus all week. But it comes from no ancient Stoic. It comes from a twentieth-century American Christian. Today: serenity.
screen: `A KITCHEN MAGNET.` → `A CHURCH BASEMENT CIRCLE.` → `THREE LINES, SAID ALOUD.`

segments.voice: The prayer is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, an American Protestant theologian who taught in New York. Scholars have argued about its origins, but the best evidence points to Niebuhr using it in sermons and talks from the early 1930s on. It asks God for three gifts. Serenity, to accept the things that cannot be changed. Courage, to change the things that can. And wisdom, to know the one from the other. Later, Alcoholics Anonymous took it up, and in AA and other recovery groups it is often said aloud together at the close of a meeting. Now, lay it beside this week. Epictetus drew two columns: up to us, not up to us. The prayer asks for a strength for each column. For the not-mine column, serenity: not giving up, but setting down. For the mine column, courage, because the things we can change are often the ones we're afraid to touch: the hard conversation, the first meeting, the apology. And then the third gift, which may be the hardest: wisdom to know the difference. That's the sorting itself. Epictetus draws the line cleanly on the page; in a real week, finding it takes work. For the people who pray it, this is a prayer to God, and the gifts come from God. On this path we don't rewrite anyone's prayer. We only notice that a Christian theologian and a Stoic teacher, many centuries apart, stood at a similar crossroads, and both said it takes wisdom to choose the road.
screen: `REINHOLD NIEBUHR, THE 1930s.` · `SERENITY, COURAGE, WISDOM.` · `A STRENGTH FOR EACH COLUMN.` · `THE HARDEST GIFT IS THE SORTING.` · then, large: `KNOW THE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it in your own words. Not as a new prayer; as a plain sentence about your own life. Settle, and breathe. Bring one situation to mind. Then finish three sentences inside. The part of this I can't change is. The part I can change is. The way I'll tell them apart is. If you pray, you can say the prayer itself, in the words you know. Then breathe, and let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Serenity. Calm acceptance of what can't be changed, the first of three gifts in Niebuhr's prayer. Today's word.
Your line: know the difference. Today, at one stuck moment, pause and ask: is this a moment for serenity, or for courage? Know the difference, then act on it. Day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Other people's opinions
115.hook: what others think is on their side of the line; how we treat them is on ours (Enchiridion 1)
115.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often treat reputation as not up to them, following Enchiridion 1, and turn their attention to their own judgments and how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart. Your line was know the difference. Was there a moment you had to choose between accepting and changing? Day one hundred fifteen.

You post a photo and check it again, and again, before the hour is up. You say something in a meeting and spend the evening replaying the face your colleague made. A relative says, at dinner, so you're still doing that job? And it rattles around in your head for a week. Other people's opinions of us are something we try hard to steer, and have very little grip on. Epictetus put them on his list, and his line runs right through the middle of the dinner table. Today: other people's opinions.
screen: `CHECKED AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` → `THE FACE IN THE MEETING.` → `STILL DOING THAT JOB?`

segments.voice: Go back to the first lines of the Handbook. On the not-up-to-us list, right after the body and property, Epictetus puts reputation: what other people think and say of us. On the up-to-us list, first of all, he puts our own opinions and judgments. That's the line. Their opinion of me: their side. My opinion, and what I do next: my side. Marcus Aurelius noticed how odd we are about this. He wonders, in the Meditations, how it is that each of us loves ourselves more than anyone else, and yet cares more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves. Epictetus adds a sharp practical point elsewhere in the Handbook. If someone speaks badly of you, don't defend yourself; he says, in paraphrase, answer that they clearly didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. It's a joke, and it's also freedom. Now, the line has two sides, and the second matters as much as the first. Their opinion is theirs to think. But how you treat them is yours. Letting go of what someone thinks is not the same as not caring about them. You can let your relative's comment stay theirs, and still pass the potatoes warmly, still ask how their knee is. In fact, it's easier. When you stop trying to win their verdict, your hands are free to be kind. And if the criticism has something true in it, that's yours to use, quietly, without needing them to see you do it.
screen: `REPUTATION: NOT UP TO US.` · `MARCUS: WE LOVE OURSELVES MOST.` · `THEY DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `HOW I TREAT THEM IS MINE.` · then, large: `THEIRS TO THINK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one opinion stay theirs. Sit back, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one opinion someone holds of you that bothers you. A comment, a look, a silence. Notice where you feel it in your body. Then, on an out-breath, picture handing it back across the table: that's yours to think. Ask one question: is there anything true in it I can use? If yes, keep that small piece. Set the rest down. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Enchiridion. Epictetus's Handbook, where he puts their opinion of you on their side of the line, and how you treat them on yours. Today's word.

Your line: theirs to think. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing what someone thinks of you, say inside: theirs to think. Then turn to the part that's yours: how you'll treat them next. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: The body is on loan
116.hook: Epictetus lists even the body among things not fully ours (Enchiridion 1)
116.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat the body as not fully theirs, following Enchiridion 1 and 11: they care for it steadily and try to meet illness and aging without outrage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Enchiridion, their opinion on their side of the line. Your line was theirs to think. Did you hand one back across the table? Day one hundred sixteen.

A friend lends you her car for the weekend, and something changes in the driver's seat. The fries stay in the bag. The mirrors get checked twice. The tank goes back full, maybe after a trip through the car wash. Nobody asked for any of it. A borrowed thing gets a different kind of care. Now here's a strange thought from Epictetus, the last one of our week on control. What if your body is more like the borrowed car than the one you own? Today: the body is on loan.
screen: `A FRIEND'S CAR.` → `NO FRIES, MIRRORS TWICE.` → `WHAT IF THE BODY IS BORROWED?`

segments.voice: Remember the first lines of the Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not. The very first thing on the not-up-to-us list is the body. At first that sounds wrong. My body is the most mine thing there is. But think about it the way Epictetus did. You didn't choose its height, or its genes, or when it catches a cold. You can't order your knee to stop hurting or your hair to stay. It ages on its own schedule. You live in it, you steer it, you're responsible for it. But you don't fully command it. Later in the Handbook, Epictetus gives the picture that goes with this. Never say about anything, I have lost it, he says, in paraphrase; say instead, I have given it back. The things we have are given for a time, like a traveler's room at an inn: use it well while you're there, and don't pretend it's yours forever. Here's the surprise. This isn't a reason to neglect the body. It's the reason to care for it well. The borrowed car gets the careful driving. When the body is on loan, sleep, water, a walk, the vegetables, the checkup: these aren't vanity, and they aren't punishment. They're how a good guest treats a borrowed thing. And the loan helps with the other side too. When the knee hurts or the mirror shows a new gray hair, you can meet it with less outrage. That part was never yours to command. What's yours is how you care for it, and how you meet what it does.
screen: `FIRST ON THE NOT-MINE LIST: THE BODY.` · `YOU STEER IT; YOU DON'T COMMAND IT.` · `NOT LOST: GIVEN BACK.` · `CARE FOR IT LIKE A BORROWED THING.` · then, large: `ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your body like a borrowed thing. Settle, and breathe. Move your attention slowly through the body: feet, legs, belly, chest, hands, shoulders, face. Notice it the way you'd look over a borrowed car: with interest, not judgment. Where is it tired? Where does it ache? Then ask: what's one thing a good guest would do for it today? Water, sleep, a stretch, a walk. Choose one. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Handbook. Epictetus's book, where the body is listed among things not fully ours, which is why it deserves careful keeping. Today's word.

Your line: on loan. Today, do the one thing a good guest would do for this body. And this week's six lines, from mine or not mine to on loan, all ask the same question. Tomorrow, a new week: gratitude. Day one hundred sixteen.

117.title: Three good things
117.hook: writing three good things each night was linked to more happiness in a 2005 study (Seligman et al.), with modest effects
117.howItsDone: The three good things exercise is widely used in positive psychology courses and therapy: each night for a week or longer, people write three things that went well that day and why each happened.

segments.voice: Yesterday Epictetus closed our week on control: even the body is borrowed. Your line was on loan. What did you do for it, as a good guest would? Day one hundred seventeen.

Here's something your brain does without asking you. At the end of the day, it hands you a summary. And the summary is biased. The rude driver makes the highlights. The late bus makes the highlights. The perfectly fine lunch, the stranger who held the door, the song you liked on the radio: cut for time. Psychologists have a name for this lean toward the bad, the negativity bias, and it's probably kept our ancestors alive. But it doesn't make for a fair report. A new week, on gratitude, starts with an exercise simple enough to seem silly. Today: three good things.
screen: `THE BRAIN'S DAILY SUMMARY.` → `THE RUDE DRIVER MAKES IT.` → `THE HELD DOOR DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: In 2005, the psychologist Martin Seligman and his colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania ran an online study of several simple exercises. One of them went like this. Every night for one week, write down three things that went well today, and for each one, why it happened. That's all. No journal, no ritual. Three things and a reason. Compared with a placebo exercise, where people wrote about early memories, the three good things group reported being a bit happier and a bit less depressed, and here's the surprise: the difference was still showing up six months later, especially in people who kept doing it on their own. Now, the honest part. The effects were modest. Later studies have found smaller, mixed results, and nobody should expect a nightly list to fix a hard life. It isn't a cure, and gratitude that's forced on someone in pain can hurt. We'll come back to that later this week. But the exercise does something clever. It works directly against the bias. The brain's summary cuts the good bits; this puts them back in. And the second half, why did it happen, matters. It makes you notice the causes: that you asked for help, that a friend thought of you, that you went outside. It turns good luck into something you can see, and sometimes repeat. Many traditions teach gratitude as a duty or a prayer. This one is a small experiment anyone can run, tonight, on the back of a receipt.
screen: `SELIGMAN, 2005.` · `THREE THINGS, AND WHY.` · `MODEST, BUT LASTING.` · `PUTTING THE GOOD BITS BACK.` · then, large: `THREE GOOD THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write three tonight. For now, a rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day, and find one thing that went well. Small counts. A good coffee, a text, a moment of quiet. Then ask: why did it happen? Stay with it a breath or two. Then find a second. Then a third. Tonight, write them down, with the why. The bell holds the time.
Seligman. The psychologist whose study had people write three things that went well each night, and why. Today's word.
Your line: notice why it happened. Tonight, before sleep, write three good things from today, and next to each, one short why. Paper, phone, the back of a receipt. Day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Counting blessings
118.hook: Emmons and McCullough (2003) found weekly gratitude lists brought small lifts in wellbeing
118.howItsDone: Some therapists and wellbeing courses use gratitude lists, often a few things written once a week, drawing in part on Emmons and McCullough's 2003 studies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seligman's study, and why each thing happened. Your line was notice why it happened. Did you write them last night? Was one of them a surprise? Day one hundred eighteen.

Count your blessings. Grandmothers say it, usually across a kitchen table. There's an old gospel hymn with that title from 1897. It's said so often that it can sound like a way of telling someone to stop complaining. So in the early 2000s, two psychologists decided to find out whether it actually does anything. They took the grandmother's advice, and put it into a study with a control group. Today: counting blessings.
screen: `COUNT YOUR BLESSINGS.` → `GRANDMOTHERS AND HYMNS.` → `PUT TO THE TEST.`

segments.voice: The psychologists were Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, and their paper appeared in 2003 under the title Counting Blessings Versus Burdens. In their first study, college students were split into three groups. Once a week, for ten weeks, one group wrote down up to five things they were grateful for. A second group wrote down five hassles, the irritations of the week. A third group simply wrote five events that had affected them. At the end, the gratitude group felt better about their lives as a whole and more hopeful about the week ahead, and they reported fewer physical complaints. They even said they'd spent more time exercising. Later studies in the same paper, including one with people living with neuromuscular disease, found similar small lifts. That word small is important. These were modest changes, not transformations. What's interesting is the comparison. Nobody gave the hassles group harder weeks; they simply spent their attention on the burdens. The gratitude group spent the same few minutes on the blessings. Same life, same week, different count. The grandmother was right about one thing and wrong about another. Counting doesn't make problems go away. But what you count is what you notice, and what you notice starts to shape the story you tell about your life. Notice also: the first study was weekly, not daily. Once a week, a few minutes, was enough to show a difference.
screen: `EMMONS AND McCULLOUGH, 2003.` · `BLESSINGS, HASSLES, EVENTS.` · `SMALL LIFTS, NOT MIRACLES.` · `WHAT YOU COUNT IS WHAT YOU NOTICE.` · then, large: `COUNT THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list five from this week. Close your eyes if you like. Look back over the last seven days, not just today. Find one thing you're grateful for. Hold it for a breath. Then a second. A person, a meal, a moment of rest, something that didn't go wrong. A third. A fourth. A fifth. If you get stuck, that's fine; stay with the ones you found. Then just breathe with the list. The bell holds the time.
Counting blessings. A weekly list of what you're grateful for, which brought small lifts in wellbeing in the Emmons and McCullough studies. Today's word.

Your line: count them. Today, write your five from this week somewhere you'll find it again. And the next time you catch yourself counting hassles, stop at three, and count one blessing. Day one hundred eighteen.

119.title: Thank them directly
119.hook: a gratitude letter read aloud gave one of the biggest short-term lifts in early studies
119.howItsDone: The gratitude visit, writing a letter to someone never properly thanked and reading it to them, is used in positive psychology courses and therapy, following Seligman and colleagues' 2005 study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: counting blessings, five from the week. Your line was count them. Did you stop counting hassles long enough to count one blessing? Day one hundred nineteen.

Somewhere in your past is a person who changed your life and was never properly thanked. A teacher who saw something in you. A neighbor who drove you to the hospital. A coach, an aunt, a friend who stayed on the phone until 3am. It's easy to tell other people about someone like that. Telling them is another matter. The last two days, the thanks stayed inside you, on a list. Today it goes somewhere. Today: thank them directly.
screen: `THE TEACHER WHO SAW YOU.` → `NEVER PROPERLY THANKED.` → `TODAY IT GOES SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the same 2005 study that tested three good things, Martin Seligman's team tried another exercise, called the gratitude visit. You write a letter to someone who was especially kind to you but was never properly thanked. Then you deliver it in person, and, if you can, read it aloud to them. Of all the exercises in that study, this one produced the biggest boost in happiness in the short run, a clear jump right after the visit. The lift held for about a month, then faded. That's worth knowing: a single gratitude visit is a big wave, not a new tide. A later study, by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, found something else. When letter writers were asked to predict how the person would feel getting their letter, they guessed too low. They expected it to be awkward, or not to matter much. The people receiving the letters reported being more pleased, and less awkward, than the writers predicted. The researchers suggest this misjudgment may keep people from saying thanks at all. What the research adds is a push to do it on purpose, in words, with some detail. Not thanks for everything. What exactly they did, and what difference it made. Detail is what makes a thank-you land. And it doesn't have to be a long letter. Three honest lines, said to them, count.
